doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Boogie-woogie and early classical lessons in Cincinnati
summary: At three he fell for boogie-woogie watching Sugar Chile Robinson with Basie; his father's pit-musician friend showed him a pattern and he entered the Cincinnati Conservatory at four.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well when you started out, was there a bit of a boogie-woogie craze when you were a kid, playing piano?

I would think so. That’s how I got influenced. I saw a little kid, Sugar Chile Robinson with the Basie Band. My parents used to take me to stage shows at the Albee and the Shubert Theater in Cincinnati. So there’s be a show like Blackstone the Magician, the Count Basie Band, and he had Sugar Chile Robinson. And I fell in love with boogie- woogie watching that kid play. I was three years old. So I came home and started to pick it out on the piano. And my dad was a professional, or semi-professional bass player. He knew this lady, Catherine Rank, that played in the pit. And she showed me a boogie- woogie pattern on the piano so I started playing. At four years old they took me to the Cincinnati Conservatory. Then it was like all classical music. But I was playing boogie- woogie. I won a talent contest in Florida playing boogie-woogie.
Was it hard for you to stick to the page when you were learning classical music? Because you had already done a little bit sort of by ear?
I don’t remember if it was hard. I got the job done. I did whatever I had to do to play the music.
